To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the PO/AH region, where local warming produces prone body extension, is a critical thermosensitive area for this behavior in rat, and (2) the posterior hypothalamical region, where local heating elicits grooming, is a critical area for this behavior.
the PO/AH region is a major thermosensitive area that controls body extension and that the posterior hypothalamic area is the major thermosensitive site that controls grooming.
the PO/AH region of the rat brain is a critical site for thermoregulatory body extension, and that lesions of this area abolish or markedly reduce this behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of lesions in the central thermosensitive regions of the brain on thermoregulation and thermosensitive behavior.
the neural basis of behavioral thermoregulation in the rat, and with the effects of ambient heat, cold, and exercise on the thermoregulatory system.
the effects of ambient heat on behavior, autonomic responses, and brain activity in the rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thermoregulatory control is a complex system of interacting mechanisms and that the brain is a major site of control.
the thermosensitive areas of the rat brain, as defined by the present and earlier studies, are not the sole source of thermoregulatory control.
the central thermosensors, which have been localized, do not control thermoregulatory behavior, and that the thermoregulatory system is controlled by a distributed network of sensors and integrators.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
thermoregulatory behavior is controlled by multiple thermosensitive regions in the brain, and each of these regions is involved with specific behavioral and autonomic responses.

the thermoregulatory system is a distributed network of sensors and effectors, with a variety of interneurons, and with a number of specific pathways, where summation and interaction of inputs can occur.

the rat brain contains several independent thermoregulatory systems that can be activated by central and peripheral thermosensors, which are not necessarily interdependent and can be differentially affected by local warming or cooling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain has a complex system that is capable of responding to environmental heat and cold.
thermoregulatory behavior is a complex phenomenon, and it is unlikely that a single mechanism can explain it.
thermoregulation is a distributed process, with different brain areas controlling different aspects of the response.
